questions.question: What does the point-normal equation say about a displacement vector lying in the plane?
options: It is parallel to the normal vector.
It is perpendicular to the normal vector.
It must be the zero vector.

questions.question: In $a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0$, what is $(a,b,c)$?
options: A normal vector to the plane.
A direction vector inside the plane.

questions.question: What information is needed to write a point-normal equation of a plane?
options: Only the dimension of the ambient space.
A single direction vector inside the plane.
A point on the plane and a normal vector.

questions.question: How can $a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0$ be rewritten?
How is the normal vector read from $2x-3y+z=5$?
A plane passes through $(0,0,0)$ with normal $(0,0,1)$. What is its equation?
Which normal vector belongs to the plane $3x-7y+z=0$?
For the plane through $(1,0,0)$ with normal $(2,0,0)$, which equation is correct?
Does $(1,2,3)$ lie on the plane $x+y+z=6$?
options: No, because none of the coordinates is $6$.
No, because the normal is zero.
Only if the point is the origin.

questions.question: What is $d$ for the plane $2x+y-z=d$ passing through $(1,3,2)$?
Why does multiplying the whole equation $ax+by+cz=d$ by a nonzero scalar not change the plane?
options: It adds a new independent direction.
It changes a plane into a line.
It keeps the same set of solutions.
It changes the normal vector to zero.

questions.question: Why is the normal vector not a direction vector of the plane?
options: It is one of the two plane parameters, no matter which values are selected.
It must lie inside the plane.
It has to be the zero vector.
It is perpendicular to all direction vectors in the plane.

questions.question: What happens if the coefficient vector $(a,b,c)$ is zero in $ax+by+cz=d$?
options: It gives a normal vector of length one, under all circumstances whatsoever.
The equation no longer determines an ordinary plane.

questions.question: Write the point-normal equation for the plane through $(1,2,3)$ with normal $(2,-1,4)$.
Rewrite $2(x-1)-(y-2)+4(z-3)=0$ as $ax+by+cz=d$.
Which point lies on the plane $2x-y+z=3$?
Why does the point-normal equation describe an infinite set of points rather than just the fixed point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$?
options: Many displacement vectors can be perpendicular to the same normal vector.
Only the zero displacement is perpendicular to a normal vector.
The fixed point is not actually on the plane.

questions.question: Why does the equation $ax+by+cz=d$ determine the normal direction but not a unique normal vector?
options: The normal vector is unique only if $d=0$.
The normal vector must equal a point on the plane.
There is no normal direction for equations of this form.
Any nonzero scalar multiple of $(a,b,c)$ gives the same normal direction.

questions.question: Find an equation of the plane through $(1,0,1)$ with normal $(1,2,-1)$ in the form $ax+by+cz=d$.
Which vector lies in the plane direction space of $2x-y+z=3$?
